bib.title: How Well do LLMs Compress Their Own Chain-of-Thought? A Token Complexity Approach

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "How Well do LLMs Compress Their Own Chain-of-Thought? A Token Complexity Approach", Ayeong Lee, Ethan Che, Tianyi Peng (Columbia Business School). arXiv:2503.01141v2, 1 Apr 2025, marked "Preprint. Under review."

COVERAGE: All 19 pages and all 46,167 chars were read, appendices A-H included. The references were skimmed. Figures 1-9 are images, so only their captions were read. I did not run figures.py, so no figure data was checked. File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/ai-engineering/01-prompt-engineering/sources/lee-2025-how-well-do-llms-compress.pdf

Setup common to all claims: six models are named (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3.5 Haiku, Llama 3.3 70B). Three math benchmarks: MATH-500, a random 500-problem GSM8K subset, a random 500-problem MMLU-Pro Math subset. 31 prompts per model and dataset. The models are standard instruction models, not reasoning models. There is no o1 or R1 experiment, even though the intro mentions them.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Accuracy depends mainly on chain-of-thought length, not on format. Bullets, no spaces, numbers only, and Chinese all fall on one accuracy-vs-length curve.
  number: none (31 prompts, shown in Fig 1)
  setup: all models and datasets. The fit is tighter for stronger models and easier benchmarks (GPT-4o and Sonnet on GSM8K). Weaker models on harder sets (Llama 3.3 70B on MATH-500) have more prompts below the curve.
  quote: "ultimately it is the length of the chain-of-thought that matters most." and "all of these strategies result in a near-identical trade-off between response length and accuracy."
  where: p4, section 2.2
- Each question has a token complexity, a threshold below which the model fails and above which it succeeds. Assumption 1 is a(X)=1{t(X)≥τ}. Token complexity is estimated by fitting a threshold classifier across the 31 prompts per question.
  number: threshold classifier accuracy about 90% (Table 3 range 89.8-97.4%). Benchmark-accuracy prediction error Err 1.4-6.3%.
  setup: Table 3. Examples are GPT-4o 92.1% classifier accuracy and 5.0% error on MMLU-Pro Math, and Sonnet 97.4% and 1.4% on GSM8K. The hypothesis is held only for "reasonable" chains of thought, not pure whitespace.
  quote: "The high classification accuracy of ¯cπ ≈ 90% and the small discrepancy Errπ ≈ 6%"
  where: p6, Table 3
  Note: the intro says "Token complexity alone can predict the performance of CoT prompting strategies with 94% accuracy." That figure does not appear in Table 3, which shows about 90% and 6% error. Do not cite 94% without flagging this.
- Prompting to shorten reasoning cuts length with little accuracy loss on MMLU-Pro Math.
  number: GPT-4o DefaultCoT 81% at 586 tokens. BeConcise 80% at 415. OnlyNumbers 79% at 222. NoProperGrammar 79% at 189. NoCoT 42% at 10.
  setup: Table 2, MMLU-Pro Math, 500 questions. The abstract-level claim is "up to 60%" length reduction.
  quote: "DefaultCoT 81% 586 81% 324 74% 552" and "There is potential to achieve significant length reduction (e.g., up to 60%) compared to DefaultCoT without sacrificing much accuracy."
  where: p4, Table 2 and section 2.1. Full tables are in Tables 6-8, pp12-13.
- No prompt wins everywhere. OnlyNumbers and NoProperGrammar work for GPT-4o and Sonnet but not for Llama 3.3 70B.
  number: Llama OnlyNumbers 63% vs BeConcise 77% on MMLU-Pro Math. Llama BeConcise (76.6) beats DefaultCoT (74.4) on MMLU-Pro Math, and BeConcise (67.0) beats DefaultCoT (55.4) on MATH-500.
  quote: "There is no universally dominant prompt; while OnlyNumbers and NoProperGrammar are effective for GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet, they are less so for LLaMA 3.3 70B."
  where: p4; Tables 2, 6, 8
- "Be concise" is far from the achievable frontier. It gives only 1.2-1.5x token reduction, while the lower bound on tokens for max accuracy implies 2.6-11.2x.
  number: GSM8K GPT-4o DefaultCoT 266 tokens, BeConcise 190 (1.40x), upper bound 10.90x, T* = 24. MMLU-Pro Math Sonnet 324 to 227 (1.43x), bound 5.50x. MATH-500 reduction 1.16-1.32x vs bound 2.61-5.88x.
  setup: Table 4. T*(A*) is the mean token complexity among solvable questions. It is an oracle that requires knowing each τ.
  quote: "while BeConcise reduces the token counts by 1.2-1.4x, the token reduction achieved by the optimal compression scheme is 3.2-11.2x, and is especially high for GSM8K."
  where: p7-8, Table 4, Corollary 1. Caveat: the text says this is for MMLU-Pro Math, but the 3.2-11.2x range spans MMLU-Pro Math (3.20-7.36x) and GSM8K (5.00-11.16x).
- Oracle upper bound (Theorem 1, a knapsack). Under a token budget, solve the questions with the smallest τ first. The bound is unreachable in practice because it needs known τ, exactly matched length, and prioritizing easy questions. The gap to the bound is large on harder sets (MATH-500, MMLU-Pro Math) and small on GSM8K.
  number: none
  quote: "it is unlikely that any feasible prompting technique will achieve the upper bound α∗π(T) or the lower bound T∗(α)"
  where: p7-8
- Models adapt length to difficulty without being asked. Token count correlates with token complexity at Spearman ρ=0.54 for NoProperGrammar. The explicit adaptive prompt TALE-EP (guess a token budget, then reason within it) gets 0.51 and lands slightly below the simple-prompt curve.
  number: TALE-EP ρ=0.51, NoProperGrammar ρ=0.54. Correlations across prompts range 0-0.6 (CharLimit(50) 0.57, NoCoT 0.08).
  setup: GPT-4o, MMLU-Pro Math, Fig 3 right and Table 5. Also on other benchmarks, see Appendix H.
  quote: "ρ = 0.51 for TALE-EP and ρ = 0.54 for NoProperGrammar" and "it produces a slightly worse accuracy than NoProperGrammar, even though it uses more tokens on average."
  where: p8-9, Table 5 p11
- Even on problems GPT-4o can solve with no CoT, it still writes long chains. Length is higher on NoCoT-fail problems under every prompt, including length-limit prompts.
  number: none
  quote: "even though the LLM can solve the problem without any chain-of-thought, the model still proceeds to generate long chains-of-thought."
  where: p11, Fig 4
- Verifier routing approaches the upper bound. Run NoCoT first, and if the answer is wrong rerun with a longer CoT prompt (DefaultCoT or similar). It needs a perfect verifier.
  number: none
  setup: GPT-4o, MMLU-Pro Math, four longer prompts, Fig 3 left.
  quote: "This routing strategy achieves a significantly better trade-off between reasoning length and performance, and approaches the theoretical upper bound."
  where: p9
- Token complexity separates models that are tied on accuracy.
  number: GSM8K DefaultCoT accuracy 97% (Sonnet) vs 95% (Haiku). Mean token complexity 17.9 vs 42.4.
  quote: "the average token complexity ¯τπ is 42.4 for Haiku and 17.9 for Sonnet"
  where: p8
- Example for a single MATH-500 question (Sonnet): about 53 tokens is the threshold, with 2 prompt exceptions.
  quote: "all the prompts which use more than ≈ 53 output tokens correctly solve the problem"
  where: p5

LIMITS
- The authors concede these limits (Appendix A, p11): math only, with no commonsense, code, or open-ended tasks tested.
- Computing τ needs many generations per question, so it is impractical at scale.
- The assumption that τ is consistent across models and tasks may not hold.
- The set is limited to 31 prompts. Fine-tuning and iterative refinement are untested.
- The result is "most relevant for strong models on moderately difficult benchmarks".
- The authors also concede that the threshold holds only for informative chains (not whitespace).
- The upper bound is an oracle and probably unattainable.
- Not shown: no reasoning models (o1, R1, extended-thinking modes) and no fine-tuned compression. Fine-tuning is left to future work (C3oT, TALE-PT).
- The paper is a preprint, and its models are the 2024-25 generation (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5), now dated.
- Length is counted in output tokens only, and the paper reports no cost or latency.
- "Use at most k tokens" is not followed exactly: "LLMs do not always follow the prompt exactly".

BUILDS ON
- Chain-of-thought: Wei et al. 2022; Kojima et al. 2022.
- Concise prompting: Renze & Guven 2024 (BeConcise); Jin et al. 2024 and Nayab et al. 2024 (word limits); Han et al. 2024 (TALE token-budget-aware reasoning, TALE-EP/PT).
- Redundancy in CoT: Chiang & Lee 2024; Wu et al. 2025.
- Fine-tuning for short CoT: Kang et al. 2024 (C3oT); Yu et al. 2024 (Distilling system 2 into system 1).
- Verifiers: Brown et al. 2024 (Large Language Monkeys); Setlur et al. 2024.
- Theory: rate-distortion theory, with the knapsack formulation.
- Datasets: MATH-500 (cited as Lightman et al. 2023), GSM8K (Cobbe et al. 2021), MMLU-Pro (Wang et al. 2024).

CODE: No code. Prompt template (Appendix E, p14): "Answer the following question. PROMPT Question: QUESTION The last line of your response should be of the following format: 'Answer: ANSWER' (without quotes) where ANSWER is your final answer."
Table 1 prompt wordings (p2) are worth keeping: "Be concise.", "Only use numbers or equations.", "Do not use proper grammar.", "Use at most k words.", "Use at most k tokens.", "Use at most k steps.".

FIGURES (captions read from the extraction, images not viewed)
- Fig 1 (p3): average token length vs accuracy for 31 prompts, with the oracle upper-bound curve. It shows the universal tradeoff and the gap to the bound faster than prose does.
- Fig 2 (p5): left, one question's per-prompt correct/incorrect against token count, showing the threshold. Right, actual vs predicted MATH-500 accuracy. This is the best picture of token complexity.
- Fig 3 (p9): TALE-EP vs simple prompts vs verifier routing against the bound. Right panel, token count vs token complexity.
- Fig 4 (p12): GPT-4o token length on NoCoT-solvable vs NoCoT-failed problems.
- Figs 5-6 (pp15-16): tradeoff curves for GSM8K and MATH-500. Figs 7-8: actual vs predicted accuracy. Fig 9: routing on other benchmarks.
- Table 2 (p4) is the most compact comparison for a note.

PROBLEMS
- The text has internal inconsistencies. The intro claims 94% prediction accuracy, but Table 3 shows about 90%. The text says "Table 4" for the classifier accuracy and "Appendix G" for tradeoff curves, but those are Table 3 and Appendix F. Two notation slips: "Table 2 ... GPT-4o DefaultCoT 81%" vs Table 6 80.8%, which are rounding. Section 4 attributes the 3.2-11.2x range to MMLU-Pro Math alone.
- The extraction is clean. Figures and plots carry no extractable data. Equations are slightly garbled by symbol extraction, but their meaning is clear.
- No embedded instructions were found in the PDF text.
